The tool you lack is a file the manufacturer already has.

Manufacturers call these files “intellectual property.” That description may be legally useful, but it hides the transaction. A customer bought the machine. You bought the equipment and training needed to service it. Then the manufacturer kept the map (service docs, fault tables, calibration steps, connector pinouts) and offered to decide who may read it. I mean “map” literally: without directions, a perfectly passable road can function like a wall.

That wall costs small shops twice. First, you spend billable hours tracing circuits or testing procedures the maker has already documented. Second, you absorb the risk of being wrong. If the missing instruction turns a twenty-minute diagnosis into three hours, can you charge the customer for all three? If you can’t, the manufacturer has shifted its documentation cost onto your bench – and onto the customer waiting for a working machine.

The damage doesn’t stop at diagnosis. Documentation and parts pairing are two gears in the same lock. A replacement component may fit, connect, and function, but software can still demand an authorization step, a serial-number registration, or a calibration routine. If the instructions and the authorization channel remain under one company’s control, “available part” means available only on its terms (and only while its server agrees). I’m not calling every calibration a scam; some procedures can protect safety or accuracy.

We shouldn’t accept a tollbooth merely because someone painted “quality control” on it.

# A manual is a tool

A manual is a tool. If you repair machines for a living, this isn’t a metaphor: service information turns a sealed box into a set of testable systems. Without it, you can own the screwdriver, the meter, the lift, the microscope, and every expensive jig on your bench, yet still be stopped by a missing diagram or an undocumented reset procedure. The tool you lack is a file the manufacturer already has.

Manufacturers call these files “intellectual property.” That description may be legally useful, but it hides the transaction. A customer bought the machine. You bought the equipment and training needed to service it. Then the manufacturer kept the map (service docs, fault tables, calibration steps, connector pinouts) and offered to decide who may read it. I mean “map” literally: without directions, a perfectly passable road can function like a wall.

That wall costs small shops twice. First, you spend billable hours tracing circuits or testing procedures the maker has already documented. Second, you absorb the risk of being wrong. If the missing instruction turns a twenty-minute diagnosis into three hours, can you charge the customer for all three? If you can’t, the manufacturer has shifted its documentation cost onto your bench – and onto the customer waiting for a working machine.

The damage doesn’t stop at diagnosis. Documentation and parts pairing are two gears in the same lock. A replacement component may fit, connect, and function, but software can still demand an authorization step, a serial-number registration, or a calibration routine. If the instructions and the authorization channel remain under one company’s control, “available part” means available only on its terms (and only while its server agrees). I’m not calling every calibration a scam; some procedures can protect safety or accuracy.

But a legitimate calibration requirement isn’t a license to withhold the method from a competent shop. Ask what the system actually proves. Does it test whether the part works, or merely whether the installer received permission? When the lock checks permission instead of performance, it protects a market boundary – not the machine. We shouldn’t accept a tollbooth merely because someone painted “quality control” on it.

I don’t think the answer requires publishing every design secret or surrendering every copyright. A practical disclosure rule can be narrower: anyone selling a repairable product must provide the information needed to diagnose, maintain, replace parts, pair replacements, calibrate systems, and restore ordinary operation. Provide it at the same time, in the same usable form, and on terms no worse than those offered to an authorized shop (including updates and corrections).

The rule also needs teeth. Documentation should use searchable, downloadable formats; required software should run without a permanent connection when the repair itself doesn’t need one; and pairing credentials should be available through a fair procedure. If a manufacturer claims that one item must remain restricted, it should identify the specific safety or security risk and disclose everything else. “Intellectual property” can’t be a sack thrown over the whole machine.

For an independent shop, this isn’t an abstract fight over information policy. It determines whether you can quote a job honestly, train a technician efficiently, and stand behind the result. It determines whether customers have a genuine choice after the sale. We pay for the hidden hours through higher prices, longer waits, discarded equipment, and fewer viable local businesses. That’s a remarkably expensive pile of bullshit to build around a PDF.

I call the rule simple because its purpose is simple: if a company sells us a machine, it must also disclose the information required to keep that machine working. Copyright can govern copying the manual; it can’t turn repair into trespass. A part that can’t be paired by an independent technician isn’t meaningfully available, and a machine whose manual remains hostage isn’t wholly owned. Give shops the map, the procedures, and the keys. A manual is a tool, and our tools belong on the bench.
